ex-401-1.title: Sharing charge
ex-401-1.question:
Identical conductors X and Y carry charges +5 μC and +1 μC respectively. X touches Y momentarily.

(a) Find the charge on each conductor after touching.

(b) State the particles that flow between X and Y and the direction of flow during touching.
ex-401-1.answer:
(a) Total amount of charge = 5 + 1 = 6 μC

Charge of each conductor = 62 = 3 μC

(b) Electrons flow from Y to X.

ex-401-2.title: Flying aluminium foil
ex-401-2.question:
An activity involving different charging methods is shown below.

(a) The styrofoam board becomes charged in step ②. Which charging method is used?

(b) Explain why the metal tray becomes charged after it is touched momentarily in step ③.

(c) Explain why the foil ‘flies’ in the air after it is released and touches the tray in step ④.
ex-401-2.answer:
(a) Charging by friction

(b) When the tray is placed on the board, opposite charges are induced at the bottom and at the edge of the tray. When it is touched momentarily, charges at the bottom are held by the board and charges at the edge are distributed to the Earth. As a result, the tray becomes charged.

(c) When the foil touches the tray, some charges on the tray are distributed to the foil. The foil then carries like charge as the tray and is repelled upwards by the tray.

ex-401-3.title: Van de Graaff generator
ex-401-3.question:
When a Van de Graaff generator (Fig a) is turned on, a large amount of charges accumulates on the dome.

(a) A pile of aluminium foil cake cups are put on the dome (Fig b). What happens to the cups after the generator is turned on? Explain.

(b) A neutral metal-coated foam ball suspended from an insulating rod is brought near the dome (Fig c). What happens to the ball after the generator is turned on? Explain.
ex-401-3.answer:
(a) The cups fly away because they get the same kind of charges from the dome by sharing.

(b) The ball is first attracted to the dome because charges are induced on it. It is then repelled by the dome after touching the dome because it gets the same kind of charges from the dome by sharing.
ex-401-3.think: If the ball in (b) does not have the metal-coating, what will happen?
ex-401-3.thinkAnswer: The foam is an insulator. It can be polarised by the dome’s electric field and attracted towards the dome, but charge cannot move freely through it as it does through the metal coating. In the ideal insulating model it does not acquire and redistribute charge readily on contact, so the subsequent clear repulsion of the coated ball is not expected. Actual motion can also depend on surface moisture and charge leakage.

ex-401-4.title: Electrostatic forces between point charges
ex-401-4.question:
Point charges X (+2 × 10−8 C) and Y (+10−8 C) are 2 m apart.

Take ε0 = 8.85 × 10−12 C2 N−1 m−2.

(a) Find the electrostatic force FXY acting on X by Y.

(b) Find the electrostatic force FYX acting on Y by X.

(c) Now, Y is replaced with Z (−10−8 C). Find the electrostatic force FXZ acting on X by Z.
ex-401-4.answer:
(a) FXY = Q1Q24πε0r2 = (2 × 10−8)(10−8)4π(8.85 × 10−12)(2)2 = 4.50 × 10−7 N (to the left)

(b) FYX is 4.50 × 10−7 N (to the right).

(c) FXZ is 4.50 × 10−7 N (to the right).
ex-401-4.tips:
Skill

Problem-solving

Finding electrostatic force

1 The direction of F can be determined from the types of charges involved: like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

2 The magnitude of F can be determined by applying Coulomb’s law. Ignore the signs of the charges in the calculation.

Tip

(a) As X and Y carry like charges, the forces between them are repulsive.

(b) FXY and FYX are an action- and-reaction pair.

(c) As Y and Z carry the same amount of charges, FXZ and FXY have the same magnitude. As X and Z carry unlike charges, the forces between them are attractive.

ex-401-5.title: How F is related to Q and r
ex-401-5.question:
Point charges X and Y are r apart. The magnitude of the electrostatic force acting on X by Y is F0. Find the magnitude of the electrostatic force F if

(a) the charge carried by X is doubled,

(b) the distance between X and Y is doubled.
ex-401-5.answer:
Originally, F0 = Q1Q24πε0r2

(a) As Q1 is doubled,

F = (2Q1)Q24πε0r2 = 2 × Q1Q24πε0r2 = 2F0

(b) As r is doubled,

F = Q1Q24πε0(2r)2 = 14 × Q1Q24πε0r2 = F04

ex-401-6.title: Finding the charge of a particle
ex-401-6.question:
Charged particles X, Y and Z are placed on a straight line such that Y is at equal distance d from X and Z. X and Y each have a charge of +q.

If the resultant force acting on X due to Y and Z is zero, find the charge carried by Z.
ex-401-6.answer:
The resultant force acting on X being zero implies that FXY and FXZ are in opposite directions. Therefore, Z is negatively charged.

+ + −

Let the charge carried by Z be −Q.

FXZ = FXY

14πε0 (q)(Q)(2d)2 = 14πε0 (q)(q)(d)2

Q = 4q

∴ The charge carried by Z is −4q.
ex-401-6.think: How would the answer change if X has a charge of +2q?
ex-401-6.thinkAnswer: It is unchanged: Z must still carry −4q. The force due to Y and the force due to Z both double when the charge on X doubles. Their balance gives k(2q)qd2=k(2q)|QZ|(2d)2, hence |QZ|=4q, with a negative sign to give attraction towards Z.

ex-401-7.title: Finding resultant electrostatic force
ex-401-7.question: Point charges X (+10−8 C), Y (+10−8 C) and Z (−4 × 10−8 C) are placed at the three vertices of a right-angled triangle (Fig a). Find the direction and magnitude of the resultant electrostatic force acting on X by Y and Z.
ex-401-7.answer:
The free-body diagram of X is as shown in Figure b.

Apply F = Q1Q24πε0r2.

FXY = (10−8)(10−8)4π(8.85 × 10−12)(0.03)2

= 9.991 × 10−4 N

FXZ = (10−8)(4 × 10−8)4π(8.85 × 10−12)(0.04)2

= 2.248 × 10−3 N

Magnitude of the resultant force F (Fig c)

= FXY2 + FXZ2

= (9.991 × 10−4)2 + (2.248 × 10−3)2

= 2.46 × 10−3 N

For the direction of F,

tan θ = FXZFXY

= 2.248 × 10−39.991 × 10−4

θ = 66.0°

∴ The resultant force acting on X is 2.46 × 10−3 N towards the left at 66.0°

above the horizontal.

ex-401-8.title: Electric field strength at a point
ex-401-8.question:
A point charge A of +2 × 10–8 C placed at point X experiences an electric force of 2.4 × 10–3 N pointing to the right.

(a) Find the electric field strength E at X.

(b) If A is replaced with another point charge B of –4 × 10–8 C, find the electric force F acting on B.
ex-401-8.answer:
(a) E = Fq = 2.4 × 10–32 × 10–8 = 1.2 × 105 N C–1 (to the right)

(b) F = Eq = (1.2 × 105)(4 × 10–8) = 4.8 × 10–3 N (to the left)

ex-401-9.title: Electric field strength near a point charge
ex-401-9.question:
Point X is 10 cm to the left of charge Q. Find the electric field strength at X if Q has a charge of

(a) +10 nC,

(b) –5 nC.
ex-401-9.answer:
(a) E = Q4πε0r2 = 10 × 10–94π(8.85 × 10–12)(0.1)2 = 8990 N C–1 (to the left)

(b) E = Q4πε0r2 = 5 × 10–94π(8.85 × 10–12)(0.1)2 = 4500 N C–1 (to the right)
ex-401-9.tips:
Tip

When Q is positive, it repels a positive test charge. When Q is negative, it attracts a positive test charge.

ex-401-10.title: Resultant field strength (1-dimension)
ex-401-10.question:
Point charges Q1 (+40 nC) and Q2 (–10 nC) lie on straight line AB. Point Y is 0.15 m from Q1 and 0.25 m from Q2 as shown.

(a) Draw two arrows to show the directions of the electric field strengths E1 and E2 at Y due to Q1 and Q2.

(b) Find the resultant field strength ER at Y due to Q1 and Q2.

(c) A neutral point exists on AB. What is its exact position?
ex-401-10.answer:
(a)

(b) E1 = Q4πε0r2 = 40 × 10–94π(8.85 × 10–12)(0.15)2 = 16 000 N C–1 (to the right)

E2 = Q4πε0r2 = 10 × 10–94π(8.85 × 10–12)(0.25)2 = 1440 N C–1 (to the right)

ER = E1 + E2 = 16 000 + 1440 = 17 400 N C–1 (to the right)

(c) This point must be on the right of Q2. Let this point be d away from Q2.

magnitude of E1 = magnitude of E2

40 × 10–94πε0(0.15 + 0.25 + d)2 = 10 × 10–94πε0d2

d = 0.4 m

The neutral point is 0.4 m to the right of Q2.
ex-401-10.tips:
Tip

Between Q1 and Q2, E1 and E2 always point to the right, so ER will never be zero. On the left of Q1, E1 is always greater than E2 in magnitude, so ER will never be zero.
ex-401-10.think: How would the answer of (b) change if Q₂ has a charge of +10 nC instead?
ex-401-10.thinkAnswer: The field at Y due to Q₁ remains to the right. The field due to the now-positive Q₂ points to the left. Thus ER=E1−E2=14πε0(40×10−90.152−10×10−90.252)=1.45×104 N C−1, to the right. The value uses unrounded component fields.

ex-401-11.title: Resultant field strength (2-dimension)
ex-401-11.question: Two positive point charges A and B carry the same charge of 1 nC (Fig a). Find the resultant electric field strength ER at X.
ex-401-11.answer:
The electric field strength at X due to A and B are as shown (Fig b).

Consider the magnitude of E due to each charge.

EA = EB = Q4πε0r2 = 1 × 10–94π(8.85 × 10–12)(0.012 + 0.012) = 45 000 N C–1

Resolve EA and EB into vertical and horizontal components (Fig c).

ER = 2 × EA sin 45° = 2 × 45 000 sin 45° = 63 600 N C–1 (upwards)
ex-401-11.tips:
Skill

Problem-solving

Finding resultant electric field strength

1 Draw the direction of the electric field strength due to each charge.

2 Find the magnitude of each field strength.

3 Resolve the field strengths into components and find the resultant.

ex-401-12.title: Electric field strength between parallel plates
ex-401-12.question:
A voltage of 2000 V is applied across two parallel plates A and B and the distance between them is

2 cm. X and Y are two points between the plates.

(a) Find the electric field strength between the plates.

(b) Find the force acting on a charge q if

(i) it is placed at X and has a charge of +3 nC;

(ii) it is placed at Y and has a charge of –3 nC.
ex-401-12.answer:
(a) E = Vd = 20000.02 = 100 000 N C–1 (to the right)

(b) (i) F = Eq = (100 000) (3 × 10–9) = 3 × 10–4 N (to the right)

(ii) F = Eq = (100 000) (3 × 10–9) = 3 × 10–4 N (to the left)
ex-401-12.tips:
Tip

E is the same at X and Y. For a negative charge, E and F point in opposite directions.
